La violence armée secoue le nord-est de: Gun violence has long shaken northeast Montréal. In Saint-Léonard, a shooting claimed the life of Meriem Boundaoui on February 7. The 15-year-old was a victim of the violence plaguing this forgotten, underfunded neighbourhood, where firearms have become commonplace. But what is happening in these neighbourhoods, and why has it come to this? A look at a systemic problem.
« Pensons aux raisons, parce que ceux qu: “Let’s think about the reasons, because those who did this are the children of a family. They have a home, parents; they weren’t born with a gun,” said community worker Najat Boughaba to about a hundred residents gathered at the intersection where young Meriem was shot dead. The crowd nodded in agreement. Throughout the speeches, the exclamation “It’s not normal!” came up again and again in reference to how easy it is to get guns in the neighbourhood.

C’est l’intervenant du Forum Jeunesse de: It was Mohamed Mimoun, a community worker at the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel, who organized the vigil, deeply saddened by the teenager’s death. For two years, he has noticed guns circulating among young people: “ordinary kids, who have nothing to do with street gangs,” he says. “Access to guns has become very easy, and it’s known among youth that there are ways you can get one. It’s become commonplace, and the fact that it’s become commonplace creates fear in some of them, who tell themselves: ‘If the others have guns, I want one too,’” Mohamed explains.
« Avant, il fallait que tu sois membre d: “Before, you had to be in a gang. It was rare, it wasn’t possible. Now, if you want a gun, you can easily find one for $900,” he adds. Many young people get guns this way to protect themselves and pull them out at the slightest quarrel, the community worker tells us in a small room on Jarry Street, while youth from the neighbourhood’s Forum Jeunesse take a writing class.
« Ce qui finissait d’habitude par les ma: “What used to end with fists now ends with guns,” he laments. A few days later, after school, on the second floor of a building, we find youth from the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel at a community radio station, where they prepare shows, songs and poems about identity, racial profiling and more. In short, the subjects that fire them up. Seated around the table in their radio studio, Philippe Thermidor and Ali Idres, aged 26 and 25 respectively, talk to us about it, along with Asma Mokhtari, 19, and Fatima Latifa, 17, who join us on Zoom.
Le décès de Meriem à 18 h seulement, dev: Meriem’s death at just 6 p.m., in front of a neighbourhood bakery, shook them. “You can’t walk down the street safely anymore. You walk outside and you don’t know what’s going to happen to you,” says Fatima.
À l’école secondaire et dans leur entour: At high school and among the people around them, they hear about guns. “I don’t know anyone who gets them, but I hear about it. They’re not going to tell us how they got them, we just know they have them,” the student explains. Those who have them do it “for the clout,” to impress people, the group tells us. Fatima thinks the issue isn’t discussed enough in the public sphere. Asma agrees.
« J’ai déjà eu des témoignages d’amis. C: “I’ve heard accounts from friends. Some saw guns for the first time in their lives in Secondary 1. Often, they don’t want a gun, but they’d rather have one to feel protected from those who do,” Asma continues. What concerns her is the reason behind this trend in her neighbourhood.
« Les jeunes ne vont pas aller chercher: “Young people aren’t going to go get guns in Algeria or Haiti and bring them back here. We’re confronted with this right here on the territory. It’s a scourge that’s eating us away from within,” adds Philippe Thermidor, a literature student and security guard. “When we young people wake up in the morning, we don’t pick up a gun, we pick up a pencil to write. We’re asking for more pencils, more notebooks, we’re not asking for guns!” he says indignantly, referring to the stigmatization of youth in northeast Montréal. A stigmatization that creates a sense of insecurity about the future among young people in these neighbourhoods.
« Des fois, les choses qu’on vit dans no: “Sometimes, the things we live through in our neighbourhoods make us feel like we don’t really have the same chance as others,” explains the 26-year-old. “In Montréal-Nord, a 16-year-old feels the need to go to work because there’s no financial security, so he has to fend for himself very early in life, he has to survive: he arrives in a society where this way of life is imposed on him.”
Par ailleurs, pour certains, décrocher u: Moreover, for some, landing a well-paid job is a feat, especially when you’re convinced you won’t be able to escape the cycle of poverty, when you see your parents living in precarity all around you and you’re exposed to other, easier possibilities. Philippe Thermidor tells us, for example, that in high school, a friend of his, who was 17 at the time, confided in him that she was engaged in prostitution.
« J’ai reçu ça comme un coup de poing, ç: “I took it like a punch in the gut, it destroyed me inside. At her age, she felt she had to fend for herself. So the child, very young, feels responsible for taking charge of their own life. If there were more resources in neighbourhood organizations, it could compensate a little.” “It’s not just picking up a gun, there’s a whole process before you pick up a gun,” he sums up.
Ali Idres, originaire de la même ville a: Ali Idres, who comes from the same Algerian city as Meriem Boundaoui, Béjaïa, experienced the murder on an emotional level. He has a lot to say. “For two or three years now, for part of the youth, guns have been part of an ideology,” he says, adding that many get them online and without a licence. Given the increased police surveillance, Ali fears the war on firearms will turn into a war on working-class neighbourhoods. “Why are there street gangs here and not in Westmount?” he asks. He would like to see in-depth work done on organized crime and firearms trafficking in Montréal.
« On va montrer du doigt le jeune noir e: “They’ll point the finger at young Black and Arab people, but where do their guns come from? There’s a whole industry behind it.” To curb this scourge, Ali wants the problem to be tackled at its source. In his view, if many young people get guns, it’s out of anger. An anger that comes from social exclusion. “We’re not in the logic of ‘We want a few rights for Arabs and Black people, be nice, bring us into your big companies.’ For me, that’s not the model! I don’t want that for us, I want a complete change!” he thunders.
Le chercheur en sécurité urbaine Leslie: Urban security researcher Leslie Touré Kapo has worked in working-class neighbourhoods in France and Quebec. “What we’re facing today is inappropriate responses to problems that have been raised for more than 10 years,” he tells us. In his view, to tackle the gun problem, we must address issues of poverty and security. The path toward firearms or delinquency is drawn along the school-family-street pattern, he continues. “When school and family are dysfunctional, the street will function.
C’est un schéma sociologique très classi: It’s a very classic sociological pattern. And on the street, anything can happen.”
D’après Leslie Touré Kapo, il faut s’inv: According to Leslie Touré Kapo, we need to invest in what happens when school lets out. In northeast Montréal, many schools wash their hands of young people once classes end, leaving them to fend for themselves. “But who is responsible for the period after school? If it’s the police, it risks escalating very quickly,” explains the INRS researcher. “We know that putting short-term repressive measures in place produces more insecurity.”

C’est cette responsabilité à l’égard des: It is this responsibility toward young people after school that speaks to Mohamed Mimoun. The community worker tries to help teenagers who can be vulnerable to delinquency.
Par le biais des programmes du Forum Jeu: Through the Forum Jeunesse programs, he helps them build their self-esteem and independence, while encouraging them to volunteer. And it works, as Philippe Thermidor, among others, can attest. “I grew up in places where I was exposed to that. Was I tempted? Yes, but was I in it? No, because my involvements didn’t leave me time to get into shady stuff,” says the man who has been part of the Forum Jeunesse since CEGEP.
Pour M. Mimoun, c’est avec les adolescen: For Mr. Mimoun, teenagers are the ones to work with to counter the temptation of guns and delinquency. “The part we’re missing is between 14 and 17.
C’est là qu’on comprend la raison de cer: That’s where you understand the reason behind certain situations of poverty and exclusion.” In his view, there isn’t enough support in the identity-building of young people in working-class neighbourhoods. “We need to work on this need to feel like somebody by having a gun.
T’as pas besoin d’une arme pour te senti: You don’t need a gun to feel like somebody, you can become a really good person and find a lot of success in other ways. Unfortunately, there are young people who don’t believe that.” That belief is also the result of social pressure.
« Tu vas créer ta propre loi, ton propre: “You’re going to create your own law, your own way of operating, when you see that the way the system operates doesn’t include you, doesn’t recognize your chances of succeeding. And that’s what I see. There’s a gap between what these young people dream of doing and everything else, including their parents, the community sector, the institutions.” “It’s circumstances, it’s not DNA,” Mr. Mimoun reminds us.
D’après l’intervenant, il ne faut pas se: According to the community worker, what’s needed isn’t only resources, but also approaches adapted to the reality of the neighbourhoods. While the community sector prioritizes the essential needs of newcomers, the new generation has other needs. “The community sector makes the same mistakes as school. There’s nowhere these young people feel welcome.
Si on veut les aider, il ne faut pas met: If we want to help them, we can’t impose rules. We have organizations that don’t want to deal with young people who are going through certain problems.
Mon défi, c’est de les aider. Quand ils: My challenge is to help them. When they’re in a safe place, it’s this intelligence and this fragility they try to hide that will come out.”
Des constats que partagent les jeunes du: The youth at the Forum share these observations.
« Si t’as quelque chose à faire, je ne p: “If you have something to do, I don’t think you’re going to hang around and think about exploring that path,” says Fatima. “When young people are fulfilled, they don’t think about that,” adds Asma.
Quant à Ali, il demande plus de culture: As for Ali, he is calling for more culture for young people in the neighbourhoods.
